subject: anatomy
title: Laryngeal framework, muscles and vocal cords

steps.tx: The **laryngeal skeleton** comprises nine cartilages that maintain airway patency and protect the vocal apparatus. Three are unpaired: the shield-shaped thyroid cartilage, the complete signet-ring cricoid cartilage and the leaf-shaped epiglottis. Three are paired: the pyramidal arytenoids, corniculate cartilages and cuneiform cartilages. The cricoid is the only complete cartilaginous ring in the respiratory tract. Cricothyroid membrane puncture provides rapid emergency airway access.

rows: Complete ring at sixth cervical vertebra
Vocal and muscular processes for vocal cords

steps.tx: The **posterior cricoarytenoid** is the sole abductor of the vocal cords, making it the most critical muscle for respiratory maintenance. It arises from the posterior cricoid lamina and inserts into the muscular process of the arytenoid cartilage. Contraction rotates the arytenoids laterally and opens the rima glottidis. Bilateral paralysis of posterior cricoarytenoid muscles leads to unopposed adduction, precipitating acute stridor and life-threatening airway compromise.

steps.tx: The **laryngeal innervation** is supplied by branches of the vagus nerve. The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve innervates the cricothyroid muscle exclusively, which tenses and elongates the vocal folds. The internal branch provides sensory supply to the supraglottic laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds. The recurrent laryngeal nerve innervates all other intrinsic muscles and provides sensory supply below the vocal folds.

steps.tx: The **recurrent laryngeal nerve** takes distinct anatomical pathways on the right and left sides. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops around the aortic arch lateral to the ligamentum arteriosum before ascending in the tracheoesophageal groove. The right nerve hooks around the right subclavian artery. Left nerve injury occurs in thoracic lymphadenopathy or aortic aneurysm, producing hoarseness, while bilateral injury produces acute stridor.
